claim: One cluster of genes (CC0681-CC0684 in CB15; CCNA_03931-CCNA_00720 in CB15N) was very highly upregulated upon entry to stationary phase.
source: One cluster of genes (CC0681-CC0684 in CB15; CCNA_03931-CCNA_00720 in CB15N) was very highly upregulated, with two of the genes, CCNA_03932 and CCNA_03933, increasing nearly 50-fold in stationary phase relative to exponential phase, reaching levels higher than all other genes in stationary phase.
evidence: RNA-Seq data comparing exponential and stationary phase gene expression showed this cluster was highly upregulated.

claim: CCNA_03932 and CCNA_03933 increased nearly 50-fold in stationary phase relative to exponential phase.
source: One cluster of genes (CC0681-CC0684 in CB15; CCNA_03931-CCNA_00720 in CB15N) was very highly upregulated, with two of the genes, CCNA_03932 and CCNA_03933, increasing nearly 50-fold in stationary phase relative to exponential phase, reaching levels higher than all other genes in stationary phase.
evidence: RNA-Seq measurements quantified the fold-change in expression between growth phases.

claim: CCNA_03932 and CCNA_03933 reached expression levels higher than all other genes in stationary phase.
source: One cluster of genes (CC0681-CC0684 in CB15; CCNA_03931-CCNA_00720 in CB15N) was very highly upregulated, with two of the genes, CCNA_03932 and CCNA_03933, increasing nearly 50-fold in stationary phase relative to exponential phase, reaching levels higher than all other genes in stationary phase.
evidence: RNA-Seq data showed these genes had the highest expression levels in stationary phase.

claim: The cdz gene cluster contains five open reading frames in two divergently transcribed operons.
source: Careful inspection of this region of the genome revealed five open reading frames in two divergently transcribed operons (Figure 1B).
evidence: Genome analysis and RNA-seq data showing strand-specific expression patterns revealed the operon structure.

claim: cdzA and cdzB are homologous to canonical type I secretion systems.
source: The genes cdzA and cdzB are homologous to canonical type I secretion systems.
evidence: Sequence homology analysis identified similarity to known type I secretion system components.

claim: cdzC and cdzD encode small proteins (86 and 84 amino acids, respectively) with weak similarity to bacteriocins.
source: The genes cdzC and cdzD are predicted to encode small (86 and 84 amino acids, respectively) proteins with weak similarity to bacteriocins (using the Gene Function Identification Tool in KEGG) and N-terminal regions resembling the signal peptides of secreted RTX proteins (Kanonenberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Computational analysis using KEGG identified weak similarity to bacteriocins, and sequence analysis identified signal peptides.

claim: cdzC and cdzD have N-terminal regions resembling the signal peptides of secreted RTX proteins.
source: The genes cdzC and cdzD are predicted to encode small (86 and 84 amino acids, respectively) proteins with weak similarity to bacteriocins (using the Gene Function Identification Tool in KEGG) and N-terminal regions resembling the signal peptides of secreted RTX proteins (Kanonenberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Sequence analysis identified N-terminal signal peptides similar to those in RTX proteins, supported by citation.

claim: cdzI is predicted to harbor three transmembrane domains.
source: The cdzI gene had no obvious sequence homologs, but was predicted by TM-HMM to harbor three transmembrane domains, and could represent an immunity gene that prevents self-intoxication by the bacteriocins (see below).
evidence: TM-HMM computational prediction identified three transmembrane domains.

claim: YFP levels from the cdzC promoter increased dramatically as cells exited exponential phase, exhibiting ~10 fold induction at OD600 of 1.0.
source: YFP levels increased dramatically as cells exited exponential phase, exhibiting ~10 fold induction once the culture reached an OD600 of 1.0 and ~30 fold after reaching an OD600 of 1.2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Fluorescence measurements from a transcriptional reporter showed induction levels at different cell densities.

claim: YFP levels from the cdzC promoter exhibited ~30 fold induction after reaching an OD600 of 1.2.
source: YFP levels increased dramatically as cells exited exponential phase, exhibiting ~10 fold induction once the culture reached an OD600 of 1.0 and ~30 fold after reaching an OD600 of 1.2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Fluorescence measurements from a transcriptional reporter showed induction levels at different cell densities.

claim: An antisense RNA overlapping the 3' end of the cdzCDI operon was expressed during exponential phase but significantly less so during stationary phase.
source: Expression of the cdz genes may also be regulated by post-transcriptional mechanisms as we noted in our RNA-Seq data that an antisense RNA overlapping the 3' end of the cdzCDI operon was expressed during exponential phase, but significantly less so during stationary phase.
evidence: RNA-Seq data showed differential expression of an antisense RNA between growth phases.

claim: CdzC, CdzD, and CdzI were not detectable in cultures grown to an OD600 of 0.1 or 0.6.
source: Western blots of cell extracts indicated that none of these proteins (CdzC, CdzD, or CdzI) were detectable in cultures grown to an OD600 of 0.1 or 0.6, but each was easily detected once cells reached an OD600 of ~1.0 (Figure 1D), confirming their stationary phase-dependent induction.
evidence: Western blot analysis showed no detectable protein at these cell densities.

claim: CdzC, CdzD, and CdzI were easily detected once cells reached an OD600 of ~1.0.
source: Western blots of cell extracts indicated that none of these proteins (CdzC, CdzD, or CdzI) were detectable in cultures grown to an OD600 of 0.1 or 0.6, but each was easily detected once cells reached an OD600 of ~1.0 (Figure 1D), confirming their stationary phase-dependent induction.
evidence: Western blot analysis showed detectable protein at this cell density.

claim: Epitope-tagged CdzC and CdzD were detected only in cell pellets, not the cell-free supernatants.
source: Surprisingly, the epitope-tagged CdzC and CdzD were detected only in cell pellets, not the cell-free supernatants, suggesting that they are not conventional, secreted bacteriocins and instead remain cell-associated, a possibility explored further below.
evidence: Western blot analysis of cell pellets and supernatants showed protein only in pellets.

claim: The ∆cdzABCDI indicator strain began to lose viability at a cell density of ~3 × 10^9 cells/mL (OD600 ~0.9) when co-cultured with wild-type producer.
source: The indicator and producer strains maintained a ratio of ~1:1 throughout exponential phase, up to a cell density of ~3 × 109 cells/mL (OD600 ~0.9), at which point the ∆cdzABCDI strain began to lose viability, dropping nearly four orders of magnitude within ~7 hr.
evidence: CFU measurements during co-culture competition showed loss of viability at this cell density.

claim: The ∆cdzABCDI indicator strain dropped nearly four orders of magnitude in viability within ~7 hr after reaching OD600 ~0.9 when co-cultured with wild-type producer.
source: The indicator and producer strains maintained a ratio of ~1:1 throughout exponential phase, up to a cell density of ~3 × 109 cells/mL (OD600 ~0.9), at which point the ∆cdzABCDI strain began to lose viability, dropping nearly four orders of magnitude within ~7 hr.
evidence: CFU measurements during co-culture competition quantified the magnitude and timing of viability loss.

claim: A ∆cdzCDI indicator strain grown to exponential phase was killed when mixed 1:1 with a producer strain that had been grown to stationary phase.
source: Finally, we found that a ∆cdzCDI indicator strain, grown separately and only to exponential phase, was still killed when mixed 1:1 with a producer strain that had been grown separately to stationary phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), indicating that the producer gains the ability to kill in stationary phase and susceptible cells need not be in stationary phase.
evidence: Competition experiments with cells at different growth phases showed killing occurred.

claim: Producer strains lacking cdzC, cdzD, cdzCD, or cdzCDI each failed to kill the ∆cdzABCDI indicator.
source: Producer strains lacking cdzC, cdzD, cdzCD, or cdzCDI each failed to kill the indicator (Figure 2C), with competitive indices of ~1 for the indicator in each case, as also seen for a producer lacking the entire cdz cluster.
evidence: Competition experiments with deletion strains showed no killing activity.

claim: Both CdzC and CdzD are required for killing.
source: Together, these results indicate that both bacteriocin-like proteins, CdzC and CdzD, are required for killing.
evidence: Deletion and complementation experiments showed both proteins are necessary for killing activity.

claim: The putative secretion system formed by CdzA and CdzB is required for a producer strain to kill a ∆cdzABCDI indicator.
source: The putative secretion system formed by CdzA and CdzB was also required for a producer strain to kill a ∆cdzABCDI indicator (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Competition experiments with deletion strains lacking cdzA or cdzB showed no killing activity.

claim: cdzI is necessary for immunity to CdzC-CdzD.
source: Our results indicated that cdzI was necessary for immunity, because any deletion including this gene led to killing by the producer, whereas the other cdz genes were dispensable for immunity.
evidence: Competition experiments with various deletion strains showed that only deletions including cdzI resulted in killing.

claim: A strain lacking only cdzI could not be generated because this gene is essential for viability.
source: We could not generate a strain lacking only cdzI as this gene is essential for viability, consistent with it providing immunity to CdzC-CdzD.
evidence: Inability to generate a deletion strain suggests essentiality, consistent with immunity function.

claim: Full resistance to a wild-type producer was seen if cdzI was driven by its native promoter or by a vanillate-inducible promoter on a high-copy vector with cells grown in the presence of vanillate.
source: We also tested a ∆cdzABCDI strain producing only cdzI in trans (Figure 2F). Full resistance to a wild-type producer was seen if cdzI was driven by its native promoter (the region upstream of cdzC), or if cdzI was driven by a vanillate-inducible promoter on a high-copy vector with cells grown in the presence of vanillate.
evidence: Competition experiments with strains expressing cdzI from different promoters showed resistance to killing.

claim: After 20 hr of co-culturing, >95% of the ∆cdzCDI indicator cells were stained by propidium iodide.
source: After 20 hr of co-culturing, >95% of the ∆cdzCDI indicator cells were stained by PI and thus were likely dead.
evidence: Microscopy with propidium iodide staining quantified the percentage of cells with compromised membranes.

claim: Only ~10% of wild-type producer cells were stained by propidium iodide after 20 hr of co-culturing with ∆cdzCDI indicator.
source: In contrast, only ~10% of wild-type producer cells were stained by PI, a frequency comparable to that seen when CFP-labeled WT cells were competed against YFP-labeled WT cells (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Microscopy with propidium iodide staining quantified the percentage of producer cells with compromised membranes.

claim: By 71 hr, 70% of the indicator population was comprised of round, PI-positive cells.
source: By 71 hr, 70% of the indicator population was comprised of round, PI-positive cells.
evidence: Microscopy analysis at 71 hr quantified the percentage of lysed cells.

claim: Cdz producers kill cells lacking CdzI, leading to a loss of membrane integrity and, ultimately, cell death.
source: These results demonstrated that Cdz producers do, in fact, kill cells lacking CdzI, leading to a loss of membrane integrity and, ultimately, cell death.
evidence: Microscopy showing propidium iodide staining and cell lysis demonstrated membrane compromise and death.

claim: The supernatant from a stationary phase culture of a producer strain did not kill a ∆cdzABCDI indicator strain.
source: Additionally, we found that the supernatant from a stationary phase culture of a producer strain did not kill a ∆cdzABCDI indicator strain (Figure 4A).
evidence: Survival assays with cell-free supernatant showed no killing activity.

claim: Concentrated supernatant from a culture of producer cells did not kill indicator cells, even though CdzC could be detected in the concentrated supernatant.
source: We also tried concentrating the supernatant from a culture of producer cells using trichloroacetic acid (TCA) or ammonimum sulfate precipitation, or by using a centrifugal filter, but did not see any killing (Figure 4A), even though CdzC could now be detected in the concentrated supernatant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Survival assays with concentrated supernatant showed no killing, while Western blots detected CdzC in the concentrated supernatant.

claim: Killing of the indicator occurred when the membrane pores were 8 µm in diameter in a split-well setup.
source: Strikingly, killing of the indicator occurred when the membrane pores were 8 µm in diameter and able to allow the passage of whole cells, but not when the pores were 0.4 µm, which restricts the exchange of cells.
evidence: Split-well competition experiments with different pore sizes showed killing only with 8 µm pores.

claim: Killing of the indicator did not occur when the membrane pores were 0.4 µm in a split-well setup.
source: Strikingly, killing of the indicator occurred when the membrane pores were 8 µm in diameter and able to allow the passage of whole cells, but not when the pores were 0.4 µm, which restricts the exchange of cells.
evidence: Split-well competition experiments with different pore sizes showed no killing with 0.4 µm pores.

claim: Boiled producer cells did not kill indicator cells.
source: To rule out this possibility, we first killed stationary phase producer cells by boiling for 5 min before adding them, without a centrifugation step, to indicator cells. If large toxin aggregates were present in the supernatant, the indicator should still be killed, but it was not (Figure 4A).
evidence: Survival assays with boiled producer cells showed no killing activity.

claim: Producer cells pre-treated with gentamicin for 4 hr did not kill gentamicin-resistant indicator cells.
source: Similarly, we pre-treated stationary phase gentamicin-sensitive producer cells with gentamicin for 4 hr before adding them to gentamicin-resistant indicator cells, again without centrifugation. As with boiled producer cells, no killing was observed.
evidence: Survival assays with gentamicin-killed producer cells showed no killing activity.

claim: TdTomato+/Venus+ events were detected at a frequency of ~12% in a mixed population of stationary phase producer and indicator cells.
source: There were three types of events detected by the flow cytometer: TdTomato+/Venus-, TdTomato−/Venus+, and TdTomato+/Venus+. The latter, detected at a frequency of ~12% in the mixed population, likely represent cases in which at least one producer and at least one indicator cell are closely associated during passage through the flow cytometer.
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis quantified the frequency of double-positive events.

claim: The frequency of cell-cell associations was not significantly different when examining mixtures of two producers, an indicator and a producer, or two indicators.
source: The frequency of such associated cells was not significantly different when examining mixtures of (i) two producers, (ii) an indicator and a producer, or (iii) two indicators (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) suggesting that cell-cell contact is not mediated by the cdz genes themselves but rather by other genes that the cdz system effectively uses to promote killing.
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis of different strain mixtures showed similar frequencies of cell-cell associations.

claim: Cell-cell attachments were seen at comparable frequencies in exponential phase cultures.
source: Cell-cell attachments were also seen at comparable frequencies in exponential phase cultures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating that whatever mediates attachment is not specifically expressed in stationary phase and so likely does not contribute to stationary phase-specific killing by the Cdz system (Figure 2A).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis of exponential phase cultures showed similar frequencies of cell-cell associations.

claim: Epitope-tagged CdzC and CdzD were fully functional with respect to killing.
source: Epitope-tagged CdzC and CdzD were fully functional with respect to killing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), while epitope-tagged CdzI was partially functional as an immunity gene (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Competition experiments with epitope-tagged strains showed killing activity.

claim: Epitope-tagged CdzI was partially functional as an immunity gene.
source: Epitope-tagged CdzC and CdzD were fully functional with respect to killing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), while epitope-tagged CdzI was partially functional as an immunity gene (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Competition experiments with epitope-tagged CdzI showed partial immunity.

claim: CdzC has two bands in the total membrane fraction, one estimated to be ~10 kDa and one smaller.
source: For HA-CdzC, there were two bands in the total membrane fraction (Figure 5A, S4C). One was estimated to be ~10 kDa, and likely corresponds to the unprocessed form of CdzC that includes the secretion signal peptide, while the other band likely represents the cleaved, processed form.
evidence: Western blot analysis of membrane fractions showed two bands of different sizes.

claim: The full-length form of CdzC was seen in the inner membrane fraction but not the outer membrane fraction.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the full-length form was also seen in the inner membrane fraction, but not the outer membrane fraction, whereas the smaller form had the opposite pattern, appearing predominantly in the outer membrane fraction.
evidence: Western blot analysis of different membrane fractions showed differential localization of the two forms.

claim: The smaller form of CdzC appeared predominantly in the outer membrane fraction.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the full-length form was also seen in the inner membrane fraction, but not the outer membrane fraction, whereas the smaller form had the opposite pattern, appearing predominantly in the outer membrane fraction.
evidence: Western blot analysis of different membrane fractions showed the smaller form in the outer membrane.

claim: A substantial amount of CdzC was present in the stacking gel of the total and outer membrane fractions, suggesting it forms larger aggregates that cannot enter the running gel.
source: Additionally, we noticed that a substantial amount of CdzC was also present in the stacking gel of the total and outer membrane fractions, suggesting that it forms larger aggregates that cannot enter the running gel.
evidence: Western blot analysis showed CdzC signal in the stacking gel, indicating high molecular weight aggregates.

claim: The presence of CdzC aggregates did not depend on CdzD.
source: The presence of these aggregates did not depend on CdzD as they were still present in a ∆cdzD strain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Western blot analysis of a ∆cdzD strain showed CdzC aggregates were still present.

claim: CdzC aggregates were dependent on the CdzAB secretion system.
source: They were, however, dependent on the CdzAB secretion system. In a ∆cdzAB strain, CdzC was found in the cytosolic, total membrane, and inner membrane fractions but not the outer membrane, and no high molecular weight aggregates were seen in the total membrane fraction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Western blot analysis of a ∆cdzAB strain showed no CdzC aggregates and altered localization.

claim: In a ∆cdzAB strain, only the full-length form of CdzC was detected.
source: Additionally, in the ∆cdzAB strain, only the full-length form was detected.
evidence: Western blot analysis of a ∆cdzAB strain showed only one band corresponding to full-length CdzC.

claim: CdzC is found in the cell membranes, with the strongest signal seen for fractions corresponding to the outer membrane.
source: Immunoblots of CdzC, along with control blots for McpA and RsaFa, confirmed that CdzC is found in the cell membranes, with the strongest signal seen for fractions corresponding to the outer membrane.
evidence: Sucrose gradient fractionation and Western blot analysis showed CdzC in outer membrane fractions.

claim: Nearly all of the CdzC in outer membranes remained in the stacking gel under non-denaturing conditions and native gels.
source: Using non-denaturing conditions and native gels, we found that nearly all of the CdzC in outer membranes remained in the stacking gel (Figure 5E), suggesting that CdzC mainly forms large aggregates.
evidence: Native gel Western blot analysis showed CdzC in the stacking gel, indicating large aggregates.

claim: High molecular weight (>220 kDa) aggregates of CdzC were present in denaturing gels and accounted for much of the CdzC, even after samples were resuspended in 2% SDS and 100 mM ß-mercaptoethanol and boiled for 30 min.
source: These high molecular weight (>220 kDa) aggregates of CdzC were also present in denaturing gels and accounted for much of the CdzC (Figure 5A–B), even though those samples had been resuspended in 2% SDS and 100 mM ß-mercaptoethanol, and then boiled for 30 min.
evidence: Western blot analysis of samples treated with harsh denaturing conditions still showed high molecular weight aggregates.

claim: CdzC aggregates could only be solubilized by lyophilization and the addition of 90% formic acid.
source: In fact, we could only solubilize these CdzC aggregates by lyophilization and the harsh addition of 90% formic acid (Figure 5F).
evidence: Western blot analysis showed CdzC aggregates were solubilized only after formic acid treatment.

claim: CdzC predominantly forms large, insoluble aggregates in the outer membrane compartment of Cdz-producing cells.
source: Taken together, our fractionation studies indicate that CdzC predominantly forms large, insoluble aggregates in the outer membrane compartment of Cdz-producing cells.
evidence: Multiple fractionation experiments and Western blot analyses showed CdzC in outer membrane as insoluble aggregates.

claim: CdzD has both the unprocessed and mature form present in the total membrane fraction.
source: Immunoblots for CdzD revealed a similar pattern as for CdzC, with both the unprocessed and mature form present in the total membrane fraction; the mature form was also abundant in the outer membrane fraction (Figure 5C).
evidence: Western blot analysis of membrane fractions showed two forms of CdzD.

claim: The mature form of CdzD was abundant in the outer membrane fraction.
source: Immunoblots for CdzD revealed a similar pattern as for CdzC, with both the unprocessed and mature form present in the total membrane fraction; the mature form was also abundant in the outer membrane fraction (Figure 5C).
evidence: Western blot analysis of membrane fractions showed mature CdzD in the outer membrane.

claim: CdzD forms high molecular weight aggregates in the membrane fractions, but these aggregates were relatively faint in the outer membrane fraction.
source: Like CdzC, there were also high molecular weight aggregates of CdzD in the membrane fractions. However, these aggregates were relatively faint in the outer membrane fraction, suggesting that they had been solubilized during the fractionation procedure.
evidence: Western blot analysis showed CdzD aggregates in membrane fractions, with reduced signal in outer membrane.

claim: CdzI was found in the total membrane fraction, but primarily in the inner membrane fraction.
source: CdzI, the immunity protein, was found in the total membrane fraction, but in contrast to CdzC and CdzD, was primarily in the inner membrane fraction (Figure 5D), similar to the immunity proteins of many pore-forming bacteriocin systems (Cascales et al., 2007; Lagos et al., 1999) and those associated with some membrane-targeting contact-dependent inhibition systems secreted via type V and type VI systems (Ruhe et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2014b).
evidence: Western blot analysis of membrane fractions showed CdzI primarily in the inner membrane, consistent with known immunity proteins.

claim: Immunogold signal from CdzC was clearly associated with the surface of stationary phase cells, usually within a larger matrix of extracellular material that was likely exopolysaccharide.
source: Signal from the gold-coupled antibodies was clearly associated with the surface of the cells, usually within a larger matrix of extracellular material that was likely exopolysaccharide (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Immunogold labeling and transmission electron microscopy showed gold signal on cell surface.

claim: The immunogold signal for CdzC was absent in exponential phase producer cells.
source: Importantly, the immunogold signal was absent in exponential phase producer cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) when CdzC is not produced at high levels and Cdz-producers cannot kill other cells.
evidence: Immunogold labeling and transmission electron microscopy showed no gold signal in exponential phase cells.

claim: A ∆manB ∆rsaA strain was still competent for killing in a contact-dependent manner.
source: This strain was still competent for killing in a contact-dependent manner (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Split-well competition experiments with the ∆manB ∆rsaA strain showed killing activity.

claim: In a ∆manB ∆rsaA strain, CdzC was seen within aggregates and fibrils, ranging from 50–250 nm in diameter, that emanated from the cell surface.
source: In this strain, CdzC was more clearly seen within aggregates and fibrils, ranging from 50–250 nm in diameter, that emanated from the cell surface (Figure 6A).
evidence: Immunogold labeling and transmission electron microscopy showed CdzC in fibrils on cell surface.

claim: No gold signal for CdzC was seen on the surface of cells lacking cdzAB.
source: No gold signal was seen on the surface of cells lacking cdzAB (Figure 6B), consistent with these genes being required for secretion of CdzC.
evidence: Immunogold labeling and transmission electron microscopy showed no gold signal in ∆cdzAB cells.

claim: Fibrils emanating from the cell were still present in the ∆cdzAB strain, suggesting that CdzC associates with these fibrils, but is not their only constituent.
source: However, fibrils emanating from the cell were still present in the ∆cdzAB strain, suggesting that CdzC associates with these fibrils, but is not their only constituent.
evidence: Transmission electron microscopy showed fibrils in ∆cdzAB cells without CdzC labeling.

claim: CdzC localizes to the surface of stationary phase cells where it mediates contact-dependent cell killing.
source: Taken together, our cell fractionation experiments and immunogold electron microscopy images support the conclusion that CdzC, and CdzD, localize to the surface of stationary phase cells where they mediate contact-dependent cell killing.
evidence: Multiple experimental approaches including fractionation, immunogold EM, and immunofluorescence showed CdzC on cell surface.

claim: Immunofluorescence microscopy confirmed localization of CdzC to the cell surface of unpermeabilized cells.
source: We also confirmed localization of CdzC to the cell surface using immunofluorescence microscopy of unpermeabilized cells. Strong signal was seen for a producer strain expressing HA-CdzC, but not for an isogenic ∆cdzAB strain lacking the type I secretion system (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy of unpermeabilized cells showed CdzC signal on cell surface.

claim: Glycines and small hydrophobic residues (A, V, I) constitute 75% of all residues in the predicted mature form of CdzC and CdzD.
source: One obvious and striking feature was the abundance of glycines and small hydrophobic residues (A, V, I), which together constitute 75% of all residues in the predicted mature form of each protein.
evidence: Sequence analysis quantified the amino acid composition of CdzC and CdzD.

claim: A span of 24 and 25 amino acids in CdzC and CdzD, respectively, was predicted to have high aggregation propensity.
source: A span of 24 and 25 amino acids in CdzC and CdzD, respectively, was predicted to have high aggregation propensity (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Computational prediction using multiple algorithms identified regions with high aggregation propensity.

claim: CdzC and CdzD harbor extended GxxxGxxxG motifs, or 'glycine zippers'.
source: These regions of CdzC and CdzD harbor extended GxxxGxxxG motifs, or 'glycine zippers'.
evidence: Sequence analysis identified glycine zipper motifs in CdzC and CdzD.

claim: GxxxG motifs are found in many class IIb bacteriocins that are thought to be secreted from cells, forming transmembrane helices in target cells.
source: GxxxG motifs are found in many class IIb bacteriocins that are thought to be secreted from cells, forming transmembrane helices in target cells (Nissen-Meyer et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to prior work describes GxxxG motifs in class IIb bacteriocins.

claim: Glycine zippers are found in some transmembrane proteins.
source: Glycine zippers are also found in some transmembrane proteins (Kim et al., 2005) and they are also thought to drive the oligomerization of certain prions and amyloid-forming proteins, such as the Aß amyloid peptide in Alzheimer's disease (Decock et al., 2016; Fonte et al., 2011) and the human prion protein PrP (Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: Citations to prior work describe glycine zippers in transmembrane proteins.

claim: Glycine zippers are thought to drive the oligomerization of certain prions and amyloid-forming proteins, such as the Aß amyloid peptide in Alzheimer's disease and the human prion protein PrP.
source: Glycine zippers are also found in some transmembrane proteins (Kim et al., 2005) and they are also thought to drive the oligomerization of certain prions and amyloid-forming proteins, such as the Aß amyloid peptide in Alzheimer's disease (Decock et al., 2016; Fonte et al., 2011) and the human prion protein PrP (Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: Citations to prior work describe glycine zippers in amyloid proteins.

claim: In the GxxxG motifs of CdzC and CdzD, the x residues were exclusively small hydrophobic residues.
source: In other proteins with glycine zipper motifs, the x in GxxxG can be any residue, with an enrichment for hydrophobic residues (Senes et al., 2000). In the case of CdzC and CdzD they were exclusively small hydrophobic residues.
evidence: Sequence analysis identified the identity of residues in the GxxxG motifs.

claim: C. segnis was killed by a wild-type C. crescentus producer, but not by a ∆cdz strain.
source: C. segnis was killed by a wild-type C. crescentus producer, but not by a ∆cdz strain.
evidence: Competition experiments showed C. segnis was killed by wild-type but not ∆cdz C. crescentus.

claim: The inhibitory effect of C. crescentus on C. segnis was ~3 orders of magnitude weaker than that observed with a ∆cdzABCDI C. crescentus indicator.
source: The inhibitory effect, however, was ~3 orders of magnitude weaker than that observed with a ∆cdzABCDI C. crescentus indicator competed against the same producer.
evidence: Competition experiments quantified the magnitude of killing for C. segnis compared to C. crescentus indicator.

claim: B. subvibrioides was killed by a wild-type C. crescentus producer, but not by a ∆cdz strain.
source: B. subvibrioides was also killed by a wild-type C. crescentus producer, but not by a ∆cdz strain.
evidence: Competition experiments showed B. subvibrioides was killed by wild-type but not ∆cdz C. crescentus.

claim: A. excentricus was not inhibited by C. crescentus.
source: In contrast, A. excentricus was not inhibited by C. crescentus, and neither were the α-proteobacteria Rhodobacter sphaeroides, Sinorhizobium meliloti and Agrobacterium tumefaciens.
evidence: Competition experiments showed no killing of A. excentricus by C. crescentus.

claim: Rhodobacter sphaeroides, Sinorhizobium meliloti and Agrobacterium tumefaciens were not inhibited by C. crescentus.
source: In contrast, A. excentricus was not inhibited by C. crescentus, and neither were the α-proteobacteria Rhodobacter sphaeroides, Sinorhizobium meliloti and Agrobacterium tumefaciens.
evidence: Competition experiments showed no killing of these species by C. crescentus.

claim: E. coli was not killed by C. crescentus.
source: Similarly, the γ-proteobacterium E. coli was not killed by C. crescentus.
evidence: Competition experiments showed no killing of E. coli by C. crescentus.

claim: An iterative computational search produced a multiple sequence alignment of 239 unique Cdz-like protein hits.
source: Two iterations produced a multiple sequence alignment of 239 unique hits, each exhibiting several of the key features of CdzC and CdzD: (i) 60–151 residues long, (ii) a predicted secretion leader peptide ending in G[G/A/S], (iii) one or two glycine-zipper motifs flanked, but not interrupted, by a proline or charged residue, and (iv) a short, charged or polar C-terminal region.
evidence: Computational search using HMM and jackhmmer identified 239 Cdz-like proteins with specific features.

claim: Cdz-like systems are widespread in bacteria, particularly in γ-proteobacteria.
source: The phylogenetic distribution of the candidate Cdz-like systems identified (Figure 7B, Supplementary file 1) suggested that this type of contact-dependent inhibition system is widespread in bacteria, particularly in γ-proteobacteria.
evidence: Computational search identified Cdz-like systems across many bacterial species, with enrichment in γ-proteobacteria.

claim: Potential Cdz-like systems were identified in clinical isolates of human pathogens such as Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Serratia marcescens, and Burkholderia cepacia.
source: Notably, we identified several potential Cdz-like systems in clinical isolates of human pathogens such as Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Serratia marcescens, and Burkholderia cepacia.
evidence: Computational search identified Cdz-like systems in genomes of these pathogens.

claim: Some plant pathogens of important agricultural crops carry Cdz-like clusters, including Xylella fastidiosa and Erwinia sp.
source: Some plant pathogens of important agricultural crops also carry Cdz-like clusters, including Xylella fastidiosa and Erwinia sp.
evidence: Computational search identified Cdz-like systems in genomes of these plant pathogens.

claim: Most putative contact-dependent systems were predicted to encode a single Cdz-like toxin protein.
source: Unlike in Caulobacter crescentus, most of these putative contact-dependent systems were predicted to encode a single Cdz-like toxin protein, with 14% having two adjacent proteins as in Caulobacter, and 5% encoding three potential toxins.
evidence: Computational analysis of identified Cdz-like systems quantified the number of toxin genes.

claim: Many of the Cdz-like systems identified were likely to have been horizontally acquired as they were often flanked by transposase genes.
source: Many of the Cdz-like systems identified were likely to have been horizontally acquired as they were often flanked by transposase genes, and most were present in only some isolates of a given species.
evidence: Genomic context analysis showed transposase genes near Cdz-like systems, suggesting horizontal gene transfer.

claim: Most Cdz-like systems were present in only some isolates of a given species.
source: Many of the Cdz-like systems identified were likely to have been horizontally acquired as they were often flanked by transposase genes, and most were present in only some isolates of a given species.
evidence: Computational analysis showed variable presence of Cdz-like systems across isolates of the same species.

claim: Many of the genomic regions containing Cdz-like systems include genes involved in cell-cell adhesion such as thin aggregative fimbriae (Tafi).
source: Interestingly, many of the genomic regions identified, though not the cdz cluster in C. crescentus, also include genes involved in cell-cell adhesion such as thin aggregative fimbriae (Tafi), which could facilitate contact-dependent delivery of the toxins.
evidence: Genomic context analysis identified adhesion genes near Cdz-like systems.

claim: The Cdz system in C. crescentus represents a new type of two-peptide bacteriocin that differs substantially from previously described, canonical systems involving secreted, diffusible toxins.
source: Our results suggest that the Cdz system in C. crescentus represents a new type of two-peptide bacteriocin that differs substantially from the previously described, canonical systems involving secreted, diffusible toxins.
evidence: Multiple experimental results showing cell-associated toxins and contact-dependent killing distinguish Cdz from canonical bacteriocins.

claim: The Cdz system is massively induced upon entry to stationary phase.
source: The Cdz system is massively induced upon entry to stationary phase and drives a nearly complete killing of any neighboring cells lacking the CdzI immunity protein.
evidence: RNA-Seq, transcriptional reporter, and Western blot data showed strong induction in stationary phase.

claim: The Cdz system drives a nearly complete killing of any neighboring cells lacking the CdzI immunity protein.
source: The Cdz system is massively induced upon entry to stationary phase and drives a nearly complete killing of any neighboring cells lacking the CdzI immunity protein.
evidence: Competition experiments showed nearly four orders of magnitude reduction in indicator cell viability.

claim: The Cdz system is the first contact-dependent inhibition system described involving a type I secretion system.
source: To the best of our knowledge, the Cdz system is the first contact-dependent inhibition system described involving a type I secretion system, as most rely on type V-based systems also known as two-partner secretion systems, or on type VI secretion systems (Russell et al., 2014b; Willett et al., 2015).
evidence: Literature review and comparison to known contact-dependent systems shows Cdz uses a unique secretion mechanism.

claim: Most bacteriocins are secreted into the environment through a type I secretion system.
source: Most small bacteriocins are secreted into the environment through a type I secretion system (De Kwaadsteniet et al., 2006; Rebuffat, 2011).
evidence: Citations to prior work describe type I secretion systems for bacteriocins.

claim: Bacteriocin gene clusters generally contain all of the genes necessary for their synthesis, modification, and secretion, along with an immunity gene.
source: Bacteriocins can be encoded on plasmids or in chromosomal gene clusters that generally contain all of the genes necessary for their synthesis, modification, and secretion, along with an immunity gene that protects the producer cell from self-intoxication.
evidence: General knowledge about bacteriocin gene cluster organization.

claim: Many bacteriocins insert into the membranes of target cells, producing pores that alter cytosolic membrane permeability, causing the leakage of cellular contents, loss of membrane potential, and eventual cell death.
source: However, many insert into the membranes of target cells, either alone or by associating with integral membrane proteins, producing pores that alter cytosolic membrane permeability, causing the leakage of cellular contents, loss of membrane potential, and eventual cell death (Cotter et al., 2013; Rebuffat, 2011; Vassiliadis et al., 2011).
evidence: Citations to prior work describe pore-forming mechanisms of bacteriocins.

claim: Caulobacter crescentus is an α-proteobacterium that thrives in nutrient-poor aquatic conditions.
source: For instance, Caulobacter crescentus is an α-proteobacterium that thrives in nutrient-poor aquatic conditions (Poindexter, 1981) where a secreted bacteriocin would be quickly washed away or diluted, making it ineffective in killing neighboring cells (Aguirre-von-Wobeser et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to prior work describes the ecology of C. crescentus.

claim: In nutrient-poor aquatic conditions, a secreted bacteriocin would be quickly washed away or diluted, making it ineffective in killing neighboring cells.
source: For instance, Caulobacter crescentus is an α-proteobacterium that thrives in nutrient-poor aquatic conditions (Poindexter, 1981) where a secreted bacteriocin would be quickly washed away or diluted, making it ineffective in killing neighboring cells (Aguirre-von-Wobeser et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation and logical reasoning about diffusion in aquatic environments.

claim: The production of a secreted toxin renders a population of cells sensitive to the proliferation of cheaters that do not pay the energetic cost of producing the toxin, but benefit from its production by others.
source: Additionally, the production of a secreted toxin, or any 'public good', also renders a population of cells sensitive to the proliferation of so-called cheaters that do not pay the energetic cost of producing the toxin, but benefit from its production by others (Riley and Gordon, 1999; Travisano and Velicer, 2004).
evidence: Citations to prior work describe the cheater problem with public goods.

claim: Contact-dependent growth inhibition systems are found in many Gram-negative pathogens in which a CdiA toxin is anchored to the outer membrane via a type V secretion mechanism.
source: This includes the contact-dependent growth inhibition systems found in many Gram-negative pathogens in which a CdiA toxin is anchored to the outer membrane via a type V secretion mechanism, and then delivered directly to a target cell (Aoki et al., 2005, 2010).
evidence: Citations to prior work describe CDI systems.

claim: Type VI and VII secretion systems are often used to deliver toxins to direct neighbors.
source: Similarly, type VI and VII secretion systems are often used to deliver toxins to direct neighbors (Cao et al., 2016; Hood et al., 2010; Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: Citations to prior work describe type VI and VII secretion systems for toxin delivery.

claim: Homologs of contact-dependent inhibition systems are absent from the C. crescentus genome.
source: Homologs of these proximity- or contact-dependent inhibition systems are absent from the C. crescentus genome (Marks et al., 2010).
evidence: Citation to prior work and genome analysis shows absence of known CDI systems.

claim: No social behavior or cell-cell interaction system such as quorum-sensing has been previously described for Caulobacter.
source: In fact, aside from an ability to adhere together and form biofilms, no social behavior or cell-cell interaction system such as quorum-sensing has been previously described for Caulobacter.
evidence: Literature review indicates no prior reports of social behaviors in Caulobacter.

claim: CdzC/D kill cells lacking the immunity protein CdzI by forming pores in the membrane of target cells.
source: Our fluorescence microscopy studies (Figure 3) suggest that CdzC/D kill cells lacking the immunity protein CdzI by forming pores in the membrane of target cells, a common mechanism of action for bacteriocins (Rebuffat, 2011).
evidence: Microscopy showing propidium iodide staining suggests membrane pore formation, consistent with known bacteriocin mechanisms.

claim: The immunity protein CdzI was found primarily in the inner membrane, where it may directly antagonize CdzC/D function.
source: Consistent with CdzC/D being a membrane pore-forming toxin, the immunity protein CdzI was found primarily in the inner membrane, where it may directly antagonize CdzC/D function.
evidence: Cell fractionation showed CdzI in inner membrane, suggesting it antagonizes toxins at this location.

claim: The extended glycine zipper region of CdzC may mediate both its aggregation on the surface of producer cells and its insertion into the membrane of target cells.
source: Thus, the extended glycine zipper region of CdzC may mediate both its aggregation on the surface of producer cells and its insertion into the membrane of target cells.
evidence: Sequence analysis and aggregation properties suggest dual function of glycine zipper region.

claim: The Cdz system may represent a special sub-class of type IIb bacteriocins or a new class.
source: The Cdz system may represent a special sub-class of type IIb bacteriocins or a new class.
evidence: Comparison of Cdz features to known bacteriocin classes suggests it may be a new or special sub-class.

claim: CdzD could help promote CdzC secretion or it may seed CdzC aggregates.
source: CdzD could help promote CdzC secretion or it may seed CdzC aggregates, although CdzC still formed very high molecular weight aggregates in a ∆cdzD strain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Speculation about CdzD function based on its requirement for killing, though aggregates form without it.

claim: CdzD may participate only in the 'warhead', or pore-forming element, of a CdzC-driven aggregate, creating a pore alone or in combination with CdzC.
source: Alternatively, CdzD may participate only in the 'warhead', or pore-forming element, of a CdzC-driven aggregate, creating a pore alone or in combination with CdzC.
evidence: Speculation about CdzD function based on its requirement for killing and similarity to CdzC.

claim: CdzC and/or CdzD must be modified upon secretion, possibly by having their leader peptides removed for full activity as toxins or to aggregate.
source: It is possible that CdzC and/or CdzD must be modified upon secretion. Although the cdz gene cluster does not encode any obvious modification enzymes, as is often the case for bacteriocin gene clusters (James et al., 1992; Nissen-Meyer et al., 2011), CdzC and CdzD may at least need to have their leader peptides removed for full activity as toxins or possibly to aggregate, with only aggregates being active.
evidence: Speculation based on presence of leader peptides and requirement for secretion system for activity.

claim: CdzC was associated with fibrils on the surface of fixed cells, although CdzC is likely not the only, or even primary, component of these fibrils.
source: CdzC was associated with fibrils on the surface of fixed cells, although CdzC is likely not the only, or even primary, component of these fibrils.
evidence: Electron microscopy showed CdzC associated with fibrils, but fibrils were present in ∆cdzAB cells without CdzC.

claim: The fibrils associated with CdzC may mediate cell adhesion, with the Cdz system effectively using them for toxin delivery.
source: As already noted, these fibrils may mediate cell adhesion, with the Cdz system effectively using them for toxin delivery.
evidence: Speculation based on presence of fibrils and requirement for cell contact for killing.

claim: The pore-forming microcin MccE492 from Klebsiella pneumoniae RYC492 is thought to form amyloid-like, but non-toxic fibrils on the surface of cells in stationary phase.
source: The pore-forming microcin MccE492 from Klebsiella pneumoniae RYC492 is thought to form amyloid-like, but non-toxic fibrils on the surface of cells in stationary phase (Bieler et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation to prior work describes MccE492 forming fibrils.

claim: The toxic form of MccE492 is non-aggregated and diffusible, such that its inhibitory activity is seen only in the supernatants of exponential phase cells.
source: The toxic form of MccE492 is non-aggregated and diffusible, such that its inhibitory activity is seen only in the supernatants of exponential phase cells.
evidence: Citation to prior work describes the toxic form of MccE492.

claim: In Staphylococcus aureus, phenol soluble modulins (PSM) form amyloid-like fibrils required for biofilm stabilization.
source: In Staphylococcus aureus, phenol soluble modulins (PSM), which share some similarity to eukaryotic anti-microbial peptides, form amyloid-like fibrils required for biofilm stabilization.
evidence: Citation to prior work describes PSM forming fibrils in biofilms.

claim: When purified, some PSM variants have antibacterial activity.
source: When purified, some PSM variants have antibacterial activity (Cogen et al., 2010; Schwartz et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations to prior work describe antibacterial activity of PSM.

claim: Many amyloid proteins pass through a toxic oligomeric stage that forms pores in membranes en route to forming mature fibers.
source: En route to forming mature fibers, many amyloid proteins pass through a toxic oligomeric stage that forms pores in membranes (DePas and Chapman, 2012).
evidence: Citation to prior work describes toxic oligomeric intermediates in amyloid formation.

claim: The small hydrophobic residues in the zipper region of the Aß peptide are thought to promote ß-aggregation by creating a 'steric-zipper'.
source: The small hydrophobic residues in the zipper region of the Aß peptide are thought to promote ß-aggregation by creating a 'steric-zipper' (Chang et al., 2010).
evidence: Citation to prior work describes the mechanism of Aß aggregation.

claim: A leucine substitution in one of the glycine residues of the Aß peptide is sufficient to significantly alter cytotoxicity and oligomer formation.
source: A leucine substitution in one of the glycine residues is sufficient to significantly alter cytotoxicity and oligomer formation by the Aß peptide (Decock et al., 2016; Fonte et al., 2011).
evidence: Citations to prior work describe effects of mutations in Aß glycine zipper.

claim: The Cdz-like systems identified are not restricted to organisms from a specific ecological niche and appear to be present in a range of bacteria with diverse lifestyles.
source: The Cdz-like systems we identified bioinformatically are not restricted to organisms from a specific ecological niche and instead appear to be present in a range of bacteria with diverse lifestyles.
evidence: Computational search identified Cdz-like systems across diverse bacterial species.

claim: The importance of outcompeting commensal bacteria to establish or maintain an infection has been postulated for several pathogens.
source: The importance of outcompeting commensal bacteria to establish or maintain an infection has been postulated for several pathogens (Hecht et al., 2016; Russell et al., 2014b) and the Cdz-like systems identified in pathogens (Figure 7) could play such a role.
evidence: Citations to prior work describe competition in pathogen infections, suggesting Cdz-like systems could play this role.

claim: The Cdz contact-dependent inhibition system allows Caulobacter to avoid the dilemma of producing an expensive common good that could get easily washed away in aquatic environments.
source: The Cdz contact-dependent inhibition system presumably also allows Caulobacter to avoid the dilemma of producing an expensive common good that could get easily washed away in aquatic environments or that would render a population susceptible to cheaters.
evidence: Inference based on contact-dependent mechanism and aquatic lifestyle of Caulobacter.

claim: The discovery of the Cdz system expands the repertoire of contact-dependent inhibition mechanisms.
source: Finally, the discovery of the Cdz system, which uses a type I secretion system, expands the repertoire of contact-dependent inhibition mechanisms and suggests that such systems may be even more widespread than previously appreciated.
evidence: Identification of a new type of CDI system using type I secretion expands known mechanisms.

claim: Contact-dependent inhibition systems may be more widespread than previously appreciated.
source: Finally, the discovery of the Cdz system, which uses a type I secretion system, expands the repertoire of contact-dependent inhibition mechanisms and suggests that such systems may be even more widespread than previously appreciated.
evidence: Computational identification of 239 Cdz-like systems suggests widespread distribution.
